title: Five-terminal quantized transconductance originating from symmetric quantum fluctuations
abstract: We consider the renormalization of transport in a quantum contact by the external electromagnetic environment and show that weak quantum fluctuations from a symmetric environment can lead to a quantized transconductance in five-terminal contacts. This mechanism does not work for fewer terminals. We present an implementation of the environment and investigate several example quantum contacts where the quantization takes place.
summary: This paper theoretically demonstrates that symmetric quantum fluctuations in an external environment can induce quantized transconductance in five-terminal quantum contacts. Using a renormalization group approach, the authors show that stable fixed points exist only when there are at least five terminals. The phenomenon is physically realized by proposing specific engineered circuit geometries using beam splitters.
main_problem: The authors demonstrate that quantized transconductance (QTC) can emerge in five-terminal quantum contacts due to the renormalization effects of symmetric quantum fluctuations from an external electromagnetic environment.
main_result: QTC is possible in time-reversible environments if there are at least five terminals, leading to stable fixed points ($P_{\pm 1}, P_{\pm 2}$) in the renormalization flow. This mechanism requires careful engineering of the initial scattering state.
method: The analysis employs a renormalization group approach by solving an effective flow equation for the energy-dependent scattering amplitudes ($\hat{s}_{ij}$), analyzing fixed points, and simulating convergence using various physical setups.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a five-terminal quantum contact coupled to a symmetric Ohmic environment. Physical realizations are proposed using 2DEG in semiconductor heterostructures configured into loops (Starfish, Football, Resonator) connected via beam splitters.
key_observables: Quantized transconductance (QTC), stable fixed points ($P_{\pm 1}, P_{\pm 2}$), and the convergence of transmission coefficients towards these quantized values.
important_parameters: The number of terminals ($\ge 5$), the symmetry of the environment, magnetic flux ($\Phi$), dynamical phases ($\chi_i$), and the small coupling strength ($z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an Ohmic environment and relies on engineering the initial scattering matrix to achieve flow towards the stable fixed points.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the five-terminal setup, proposed circuit implementations (Starfish, Football, Resonator), and convergence diagrams showing how transmission coefficients flow toward quantized values ($P_{\pm 1}$ or $P_{\pm 2}$) near specific resonance crossings.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using renormalization group equations for five-terminal contacts. It then proposes concrete physical realizations in semiconductor structures, analyzing convergence diagrams based on varying magnetic flux and dynamical phases relative to level crossings (A, B, C).
why_interesting: This work connects mesoscopic transport phenomena with fundamental concepts of quantum fluctuations and renormalization flow, providing a mechanism for quantization beyond standard symmetry arguments.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The setup under consideration. A five-terminal quantum con- tact, characterized by the scattering matrix ˆs, is connected to a time- reversible electromagnetic environment described by the frequency- dependent 5 × 5 symmetric impedance matrix ˆZ(ω). The high- frequency fluctuations in the environment can develop QTC in the contact. To uncouple the contact and environment at very low fre- quencies, which is required for transport measurements, the connec- tion is realized via large capacitors not shown in the figure.

FIG. 2. The region of positively defined impedance matrices (gray) overlapped by the region of stability (hatched) for P±1 and P±2 in the space of matrix elements Zi. The stability region corresponds to amplifying Ohmic environments.

FIG. 4. Three setups proposed to demonstrate the QTC fixed points are built from beam splitters forming loops. Gray polygons represent the terminals, lines represent the propagation channels, and black n −th order polygons represent the beam splitters, corresponding to a unitary n × n matrix. In the Starfish setup, electrons follow the loop unless exiting to the terminals underway. In the Football setup, the central beam splitter provides more chances to explore the loops. The beam splitters in the Resonator have a low entrance transparency, this is indicated by crosses. If a resonance condition is achieved, this guarantees electron trapping in the loop, so that it can explore all terminals.

FIG. 3. Implementation of the electromagnetic environment. Gen- eral design. In each of the 5 loops labeled by α, the self inductances of the ideal transformers Miα, Liα are chosen to correspond to ψ(α) i , an eigenvector of ˆz. The resistor Rα gives the corresponding eigen- value. A cyclically symmetric Ohmic environment is obtained when ψ(α) i correspond to Fourier modes, and R1 = R4, R2 = R3.

FIG. 6. The Football setup. Convergence diagram. Plots (a) and (c) show the convergence regions to P±1 (black and white) for the environment E1 , while plots (b) and (d) show this for P±2 and envi- ronment E2. In plots (a) and (b) we tune the flux and all dynamical phases χ(0) i ≡χ, with χ(1) i = 0, while in plots (c) and (d) we tune the flux and the dynamical phase of one channel, χ(0) 0 ≡χ, with χ(0) i̸=0 = −π/3, χ(1) i = −π/2.
